slides.heading: How Brain-Computer Interfaces Work
slides.body: The technology turning thought into action — and what it means for the future of humanity

slides.heading: What Is a BCI?
slides.body: A brain-computer interface (BCI) is a direct communication pathway between the brain and an external device. It reads electrical signals from neurons and translates them into commands a computer can execute — no muscles required.

slides.heading: How the Brain Signals
slides.body: Neurons communicate via tiny electrical pulses called action potentials. When you think about moving your hand, millions of neurons fire in coordinated patterns. BCIs detect these patterns using electrodes placed on or inside the brain.

slides.heading: Non-Invasive vs. Invasive
slides.body: EEG headsets sit on the scalp and are safe but pick up noisy, low-resolution signals. Implanted electrodes (like Neuralink's) sit directly in cortical tissue, capturing crisp, high-bandwidth neural data — but require surgery.

slides.heading: Decoding Neural Signals
slides.body: Raw electrode data is a chaotic stream of voltage spikes. Machine learning algorithms — trained on the user's own brain patterns — learn to separate signal from noise and map specific firing patterns to intended actions.

slides.heading: Medical Breakthroughs
slides.body: BCIs have already helped paralyzed patients type messages, move robotic arms, and even walk again via spinal stimulators. For people with ALS or locked-in syndrome, these devices restore a lifeline of communication.

slides.heading: The Bandwidth Problem
slides.body: The human brain has roughly 86 billion neurons. Current implants record from a few hundred to a few thousand at once. Scaling up recording density — without damaging tissue — is the central engineering challenge of the field.

slides.heading: Bidirectional BCIs
slides.body: Next-generation devices don't just read the brain — they write to it. By sending precisely timed electrical pulses back into neural circuits, they can restore sensory feedback, suppress seizures, or treat depression in real time.

slides.heading: Ethics and Privacy
slides.body: Neural data is the most intimate data imaginable. Who owns your brainwaves? Can insurers or employers demand access? Researchers and regulators are racing to establish frameworks for neural privacy before the technology outpaces the law.

slides.heading: Mind Meets Machine
slides.body: BCIs are no longer science fiction — they're in clinical trials, restoring lives today. As the technology matures, the line between biological and digital intelligence will blur in ways we're only beginning to understand.
